metaDescription: Cordless tool battery chargers compared by charge time, cooling, multi-bay design and platform compatibility for DeWalt, Milwaukee and Makita batteries.
expertTake: The Milwaukee 48-59-1815 Super Charger is the best charger for M18 shops that need packs back fast, charging an XC6.0 FORGE battery to 80 percent in about 15 minutes. The Makita DC18RC is the best single-bay LXT charger, and the DeWalt DCB1104 is the compact pick for 12V and 20V MAX users. The Milwaukee 48-59-1812 is the value pick for crews that run both M12 and M18. Chargers only fit their own platform, so buy the one that matches your batteries.
introParagraphs: A cordless tool charger does more than push current into a pack. It talks to a chip in the battery, watches cell temperature and voltage, and tapers the current so the cells charge fast without being damaged. A good charger shortens downtime and extends battery life, while a poor one leaves you waiting.
Charge speed, cooling and bay count decide how well a charger keeps up with a working crew.

products.name: Milwaukee 48-59-1815 M18 Dual Bay Simultaneous Super Charger
products.description:
The 48-59-1815 is a dual-bay M18 charger that charges two packs at the same time. Milwaukee says it takes an M18 REDLITHIUM FORGE XC6.0 battery to 80 percent in about 15 minutes. Charge Adapt technology distributes power between the two bays for optimized simultaneous charging, and a Cool-Cycle active cooling system reduces charge time.

Active cooling matters because heat is the limit on fast charging. A pack that gets hot has to charge slowly or it degrades, so a fan that pulls heat out lets the charger push more current. Simultaneous charging is also a time saver for a crew with two tools on the go. Compared with the older Milwaukee 48-59-1812, the Super Charger is faster and charges two packs at once, while the 1812 is a sequential, multi-voltage charger.

It only charges M18 batteries. Keep the fan intake clear of dust, and use it on a hard surface, not a rug. Because it is a fast charger, expect some fan noise, and place it where it can pull in cool air. A rack or shelf near a workbench keeps the cord off the floor.
products.bestFor: M18 crews that need to turn packs quickly.
pros: Charges an XC6.0 to 80 percent in about 15 minutes
Charge Adapt splits power between packs

products.name: Makita DC18RC 18V LXT Rapid Optimum Charger
products.description:
The DC18RC is Makita's Rapid Optimum Charger for 18V LXT batteries. It charges a 3.0Ah pack in 30 minutes, a 4.0Ah pack in 40 minutes and a 5.0Ah pack in 45 minutes.

Those figures show how the charger scales: charge time grows with capacity, but not linearly, because the charger pushes more current into larger packs. An optimum charging system communicates with the battery's chip to protect cell life. It is a single-bay charger, so you charge one pack at a time, which is fine for a home shop but slow for two or three batteries in a row.

It is a simple, reliable charger. Compared with the Makita DC18SD, which also lists 25 minutes for 2.0Ah, the DC18RC is the standard LXT charger, and the DC18SD adds 7.2V compatibility. Lithium packs like to be charged at room temperature, so let a hot pack cool a few minutes after heavy use before docking it. Wipe the terminals now and then.
products.bestFor: LXT owners who want a fast, reliable single-bay charger.
cons: No cooling fan on this model per the listing

products.name: Makita DC18SD 7.2V to 18V Battery Charger
products.description:
The DC18SD charges Makita batteries from 7.2V to 18V and lists charge times from 25 minutes for a 2.0Ah pack to 45 minutes for a 5.0Ah pack. A built-in fan cools the battery during charging, and the charger communicates with the battery's chip to optimize battery life.

Cooling is the difference between this charger and the DC18RC listed here: the fan lets the DC18SD keep current high for longer. A 7.2 to 18V range covers older Makita packs, which suits shops with legacy tools. It is a single-bay design.

Keep the fan intake clean. Heat makes batteries age, so a charger with a fan is worth it if you charge in a warm garage. If you charge many packs in a row, the fan on this model keeps temperature in check. Replace the charger if the fan seizes, since a hot charge shortens battery life.
products.bestFor: Shops with a mix of older and newer Makita batteries.

products.name: DEWALT DCB1104 12V MAX / 20V MAX 4 Amp Charger
products.description:
The DCB1104 is a 4 amp charger that handles DeWalt 12V MAX, 20V MAX and FLEXVOLT batteries, with a two-stage LED state of charge indicator. DeWalt says it is 15 percent smaller than the DCB115 4A charger.

A 4 amp charger charges a typical 5.0Ah pack in roughly an hour or a little more, which is slower than rapid chargers but gentler on cells. Because it fits three DeWalt platforms, it is the one charger you need for a mixed collection. The small size helps on a truck seat.

It does not list active cooling, so heavy-use crews may want a faster option. For home use it is a good all-rounder. For a collection with several voltages, this single charger replaces three, and its compact size fits a truck console. Do not expect the speed of a dedicated rapid charger.
products.bestFor: DeWalt owners who want one compact charger for every pack.
cons: Single bay, no cooling fan listed

products.name: Milwaukee 48-59-1812 M12/M18 Multi-Voltage Charger

specList.label: Bays
specList.value: Holds one of each at once

products.description:
The 48-59-1812 charges both 12V and 18V Milwaukee batteries and can hold one of each at the same time. It charges them one after the other and communicates with a chip in each battery to track how much charge it has received.

Sequential charging means you do not manage charge cycles: the charger finishes one pack, then starts the next. An onboard fuel gauge shows status. It is a flexible charger for owners who run both M12 and M18 tools, since a single unit replaces two.

The tradeoff is speed. It is not a rapid charger, so two big packs take a while. For a crew, the Super Charger is faster. Keep both batteries clean and seated fully, because a poor connection stops charging and flashes an error. Check which battery the charger prefers when two are loaded.
products.bestFor: Owners who use both M12 and M18 Milwaukee tools.
cons: Packs charge one at a time

products.name: Milwaukee M18 PACKOUT Six Bay Rapid Charger
products.description:
The PACKOUT six bay rapid charger holds six M18 batteries and charges two at once at a rapid rate that Milwaukee says is up to 40 percent faster than standard chargers. After the first two, it automatically moves to the next pair.

Sequential pair charging is useful for a shop or truck that owns many batteries, since you can load all six at the end of the day and have them ready in the morning. It fits M18 batteries only and mounts into the PACKOUT system. A six-bay unit is overkill for someone with two batteries.

It is a storage and charging station in one, and the real benefit is organization. Do not stack it where heat can build up. Plan the layout before you mount it, since a six-bay unit is large, and give it clear space for airflow. Load all six packs at the end of the day and they will be ready in the morning.
products.bestFor: Crews with many M18 batteries who want an organized charging station.
pros: Charges two at once, then the next pair
Up to 40 percent faster than standard chargers

buyingCriteria.explanation: Speed depends on the charger's current and the pack's capacity. The Makita DC18RC charges a 5.0Ah pack in 45 minutes, and the Milwaukee Super Charger takes an XC6.0 to 80 percent in about 15 minutes by Milwaukee's figure. A 4 amp DeWalt charger takes closer to an hour. Fast charging costs more but saves downtime. Add up the minutes you spend waiting each week to decide how much speed is worth.

Heat is what limits fast charging and ages cells. The Milwaukee Super Charger has active Cool-Cycle cooling and the Makita DC18SD has a fan. A charger without cooling must slow down to protect the pack. If you charge in a hot garage, cooling is worth paying for. Hot batteries cannot charge fast, so cooling is where the best chargers differ.

A single-bay charger, like the Makita DC18RC, charges one pack at a time. The Milwaukee Super Charger charges two at once, and the PACKOUT unit holds six. Count how many packs you use in a day and choose accordingly. Think about how many packs you own, not only how many you use.

Chargers match their platform. The DeWalt DCB1104 covers 12V MAX, 20V MAX and FLEXVOLT, and the Milwaukee 48-59-1812 covers M12 and M18. A charger for one brand will not charge another's packs. Check your battery model, not only the voltage. A charger for a different generation of the same brand may not fit, so verify the battery family.

Good chargers talk to the chip in the battery to monitor temperature and voltage. Makita and Milwaukee describe this feature. Third-party chargers may lack it. Communication protects the pack from overcharge and extends its life. Reading the pack chip lets the charger stop at the right moment.

Cheap replacement chargers, such as those listed for Makita and Bauer, may skip safety circuits. A poor charger can overheat a lithium pack. For safety, use the maker's charger. If a price looks too good, check that the charger is genuine.

specDecoder.watchFor: Real charge time depends on the pack's size and temperature.

specDecoder.meaning: Charge time is often quoted to 80 percent, because the last part of the charge is slow. Milwaukee quotes 15 minutes to 80 percent for an XC6.0. It matters most when you own several battery sizes.
specDecoder.watchFor: Compare like with like, since full-charge times are longer.

specDecoder.meaning: Simultaneous chargers charge several packs at once, and sequential chargers charge them one after another. It matters most when you own several battery sizes.
specDecoder.watchFor: A six-bay sequential charger still takes hours to fill six packs.

specDecoder.meaning: A fan or airflow path cools the battery during charge. Cooler cells can accept higher current. It matters most when you own several battery sizes.
Voltage range shows which platforms a charger accepts, such as 7.2V to 18V on the Makita DC18SD. It matters most when you own several battery sizes.
specDecoder.watchFor: A matching voltage does not guarantee compatibility. Check the battery family.

maintenance.why: Dust blocks airflow and slows charging. Blow out fans with air.
Dirty contacts cause poor charging. Wipe them with a dry cloth.
Heat slows charging and ages cells.
A frayed cord is a fire risk. Replace damaged chargers.

maintenance.task: Do not leave packs on forever
maintenance.why: Long storage at full charge ages cells. Remove packs after charging.

faq.q: Can I use a different brand's charger?
faq.a: No. Chargers match their own battery platform. Third-party chargers may not communicate with the pack. Using a mismatched charger can void warranties and risk fire.

faq.q: Are fast chargers bad for batteries?
faq.a: Not if they have cooling and communication. Heat is the real enemy. A charger that tapers current and watches temperature protects cells better than raw speed.

faq.q: How long should a charge take?
faq.a: A 5.0Ah pack takes about 45 minutes on a rapid charger or an hour on a 4 amp charger. Capacity matters, since a 2.0Ah pack charges quicker than a 6.0Ah pack on the same charger.

faq.q: Can I leave a battery on the charger?
faq.a: Modern chargers stop at full, so it is safe overnight. Long storage at full charge ages cells over months. Do not leave packs charging in direct sun or an unventilated enclosure.

faq.q: Do I need a multi-voltage charger?
faq.a: Only if you run two voltages of one brand. A single-voltage charger is simpler. Check the model number on your battery before you buy any charger.

faq.q: Is a six-bay charger worth it?
faq.a: Only for crews with many packs. A home shop rarely needs more than two bays. For a small shop, one good single-bay charger and a spare pack work better.
